title: Event Triggered Execution: LC_LOAD_DYLIB Addition
summary: Mach-O is the executable format used by macOS and OS X, and a Mach-O file begins with a series of load commands that tell the kernel and the dynamic linker how to build the process. One of those commands, the load dynamic library command, records a library that must be loaded when the binary starts. Attackers can add one of these commands to an existing binary, pointing at a malicious dynamic library, so the payload executes inside the process every time that binary is run. This differs from the other trigger types in this family because the event that causes execution is the loading of one specific modified program, often a trusted system tool that other software already runs on a schedule. The change also breaks any existing code signature, because the file has been edited, so an attacker usually removes the code signature load command as well to stop macOS from refusing to launch it. Detection artefacts are strong when defenders look for them: binaries whose recorded library list includes a library outside the expected system or bundle paths, unsigned or ad-hoc signed libraries, files whose modification time is newer than their version metadata, and process telemetry that reports the libraries loaded by each process, which is available on modern macOS through the endpoint security framework.

beginner.definition: On macOS, the file that you run is called a Mach-O binary. Inside its header there is a list of shared libraries, which are helper files that the system must load when the program starts. This technique is when an attacker adds their own helper to that list.
beginner.whyItMatters: Their helper then loads, and runs, every time that program starts. The program itself looks normal and does its usual job, so nothing seems broken. Attackers often edit a common tool that the system runs often, which means their code runs often too. It is a subtle trick that survives restarts.
howItWorks: The attacker chooses a program that already runs often on the machine, such as a system tool.
They edit the program's header and add a load command for their own helper library.
That new header entry makes the system load the attacker's library whenever the program starts.
Editing the file breaks its digital signature, so they also remove the signature check entry.
When the program starts, the system loads the library and runs its startup code inside the process.
The program then continues to work normally, so the user notices nothing unusual at all.
beginner.example: Think of a delivery van with a written checklist of parts to fit before each trip. Someone adds one line to the checklist, naming a spare wheel kept in an unusual place. The van still looks and drives the same, and the driver follows the list without thinking. The extra part is fitted on every single trip.
takeaways: A Mach-O header lists the libraries a program loads, and that list can be modified.
Signatures normally catch the change, so a removed signature entry is a strong warning sign.
Compare the libraries each process loads against the ones the software should use.

objectives: Explain what a Mach-O binary and its load commands are.
Describe what the load dynamic library command does at program start.
Explain why editing a binary breaks its code signature.
Explain why attackers remove the code signature command from a binary.
Identify the telemetry that shows which libraries a process loaded.
